prompt: You're using Wiggins and McTighe's backward design process to plan a lesson. What should you define first?
choices: The slides and lecture script you'll present
The terminal, observable performance the learner should be able to do by the end, and how you'll check for it
The total number of quiz questions you'll need
Which tools or IDE the learner should install

prompt: A lesson's stated objective is 'the learner understands the Single Responsibility Principle.' Under backward design, what's the main problem with this objective as written?
choices: It's too short to be a real learning objective
It doesn't name an observable action, so there's no way to design a check that tells you whether it was actually met
It should mention the Open/Closed Principle instead of SRP
It's fine as written, since understanding is always demonstrated by a good quiz score

prompt: Sweller's research on cognitive load and the worked-example effect suggests that, for a genuine beginner encountering a new design concept, the most effective early sequencing is:
choices: Pure discovery: give them the buggy class and no example, and let them struggle to the correct split on their own
A fully worked example first, then a partially completed ('faded') example, then independent practice
A written definition, followed immediately by an independent practice problem with no example
Independent practice first, followed by the correct answer as an example afterward

prompt: In a live workshop, which of these is a concrete, real-time feedback mechanism, as opposed to 'ask for feedback' in the abstract?
choices: Sending a satisfaction survey by email after the workshop ends
Asking 'any questions?' at the end of each section and moving on if no one speaks up
A visible sticky-note system (green/red on a laptop lid) that lets you see, second by second, who's stuck, the way The Carpentries trains instructors to run it
Assuming the lesson worked if nobody complained

prompt: Three weeks after a workshop on SRP, you audit merged PRs and find that attendees are now splitting mixed-responsibility classes unprompted in real code, without being told to. In Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation, this evidence sits at which level?
choices: Level 1 (Reaction) — it just means they liked the workshop
Level 2 (Learning) — it only shows they passed an in-session quiz
Level 3 (Behavior) — it shows the skill transferred into real, unprompted on-the-job work
Level 4 (Results) — it directly proves the team's defect rate dropped

prompt: Which of these best measures whether a learner actually understands SRP, rather than just recalling a definition, per Bloom's taxonomy?
choices: 'What does the S in SOLID stand for?'
'Which of the following statements best defines the Single Responsibility Principle?'
Given a short class that mixes pricing math, database persistence, and receipt printing, ask the learner to identify which extraction correctly isolates each responsibility with none duplicated
'True or False: SRP is one of the five SOLID principles.'

prompt: In multiple-choice assessment design, why are 'attractive distractors' built from real, observed misconceptions (e.g., the common wrong belief that SRP means 'one method per class') better than random plausible-sounding wrong answers?
choices: They make the question harder to guess, which is the only goal of a good distractor
A distractor that encodes a real misconception tells you, from the choice a learner picks, exactly which specific misunderstanding they have, not just that they got it wrong
Random wrong answers are actually preferred because they're faster to write
Distractors don't affect what a multiple-choice question measures, only its difficulty

prompt: You're designing a 30-minute lesson on TDD's Red-Green-Refactor cycle for a genuine Tier 1 beginner. Why narrow the scope to 'write one failing test for one function and make it pass' instead of 'teach TDD'?
choices: Because TDD is not worth teaching to beginners at all

A narrower, concretely-scoped objective is one you can actually build a full worked example, formative check, and independent practice around in the time available — 'teach TDD' isn't an objective you can design backward from
Because Red-Green-Refactor only applies to small functions, never to larger systems
Because beginners cannot write failing tests
